terms: Buddha's diagnosis: suffering exists, has a cause, can cease and there is a path to its cessation.
Suffering, unsatisfactoriness or unease that pervades unawakened life.
Craving or thirst that gives rise to dukkha.
Cessation of craving and suffering; the goal of Buddhist practice.
Eight interrelated factors leading to liberation, grouped under wisdom, ethics and concentration.
School of the Elders, predominant in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos.
Great Vehicle, prominent in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam, emphasising the bodhisattva ideal.
Diamond Vehicle, prominent in Tibet, Mongolia and Bhutan, employing tantric practices.
Being who postpones final nirvana to help all sentient beings achieve liberation.
Tripitaka of Theravada Buddhism, preserved in Pali language.
Spiritual leader of Tibetan Buddhism; the current 14th Dalai Lama, Tenzin Gyatso, was born in 1935 and recognised in 1940.
Founder of Buddhism, traditionally dated c. 563-483 BCE (some scholars c. 480-400 BCE).
Old age, sickness, death and a wandering ascetic — encounters that prompted Siddhartha's renunciation.
Tree at Bodh Gaya under which Siddhartha attained enlightenment.
Title meaning 'the Awakened One' applied to Siddhartha after his enlightenment.
The Buddha's teaching, one of the Three Jewels alongside Buddha and Sangha.
Community of Buddhist monks and nuns; also broader community of practitioners.
Second Vatican Council (1962-65) convened by Pope John XXIII to renew Catholic life and engagement with the modern world.
Vatican II Dogmatic Constitution on the Church (1964) emphasising the Church as 'People of God'.
Vatican II Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy (1963) allowing vernacular language in worship.
1965 Declaration on the Church's relation with non-Christian religions, transforming Jewish-Catholic relations.
Italian for 'updating', John XXIII's term for the renewal he sought.
Movement promoting Christian unity, expressed in the Decree Unitatis Redintegratio.
Largest Christian communion, led by the Pope (Bishop of Rome), with around 1.4 billion members.
Communion of autocephalous churches united by liturgy and the seven Ecumenical Councils.
Family of non-Chalcedonian churches including Coptic and Armenian Orthodox.
Western Christian movement originating in the Reformation, emphasising sola scriptura and sola fide.
Tradition tracing to the English Reformation, balancing Catholic and Reformed elements.
Fastest-growing Protestant movement emphasising Holy Spirit gifts, originating in early 20th century revivals.
Christian doctrine of one God in three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
Doctrine that the eternal Son became human in Jesus of Nazareth (John 1).
Council of Chalcedon 451 affirmation of two natures, divine and human, in one person.
Christian confession of faith from the Council of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381).
Western baptismal creed summarising apostolic faith, in present form from c. 700.
Latin addition affirming Spirit's procession 'from the Son' that contributed to the East-West schism.
Ethical theory rooted in Aquinas holding that moral norms can be known by rational reflection on human nature.
'Do good and avoid evil' — Aquinas's first principle of practical reason.
Aquinas's basic goods: preservation of life, reproduction, education, ordered society and worship of God.
View that moral obligation derives from God's commands.
Plato's question: is something good because God commands it, or does God command it because it is good?
Robert Adams's view that God's commands derive from God's loving and good character.
Religious principle that human life has special, often inviolable, value because it bears the image of God or atman.
Approach weighing well-being and capability in medical decisions.
Religious framework treating humans as caretakers of creation, prominent in Abrahamic environmentalism.
Pope Francis's 2015 encyclical on care for the common home, articulating integral ecology.
Principle of non-harm or non-violence, central in Jainism, Hinduism and Buddhism, extended to environmental ethics.
Domain where religious traditions articulate norms — from Catholic natural law to liberal Protestant, Jewish and Buddhist approaches — increasingly debated in pluralistic societies.
Aristotle's notion of human flourishing as the highest good achieved through virtuous activity.
Aristotle's principle that virtue lies between excess and deficiency, e.g. courage between cowardice and rashness.
Buddhist concept of teaching and acting in ways appropriate to context and capacity.
Confucian virtue of humaneness or benevolence, central to ethical life.
Confucian ritual propriety, expressing respect and order in relationships.
Rooted in seva (selfless service), kirat karni (honest work) and vand chakna (sharing), under the guidance of the Guru Granth Sahib.
Ultimate reality, the unchanging, infinite ground of being in Hindu philosophy.
Eternal self or soul; in Advaita Vedanta, ultimately identical with Brahman.
Cycle of birth, death and rebirth in which atman is bound until liberation.
Law of moral cause and effect determining the conditions of rebirth.
Liberation from samsara — the highest aim of Hindu life.
Non-dualist school led by Adi Shankara (8th century) teaching identity of atman and Brahman.
Threefold form of the divine: Brahma the creator, Vishnu the preserver, Shiva the destroyer.
Incarnation of a deity, especially Vishnu, who is traditionally said to have ten avatars (dashavatara).
Devotional worship offered to deities at home and in temples, often using flowers, light and food.
Image or statue of a deity that becomes a focus of worship.
Festival of lights celebrated in autumn, marking Rama's return to Ayodhya and the victory of light.
Classical fourfold social order: Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra — distinct from modern jati.
Earliest Hindu scriptures composed in Sanskrit between c. 1500 and 500 BCE.
Oldest Veda, a collection of 1,028 hymns to deities like Agni, Indra and Varuna.
Philosophical texts forming the latter portion of the Vedas, foundational for Vedanta.
700-verse dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna within the Mahabharata epic.
Distinction between revealed (shruti, e.g. Vedas) and remembered (smriti, e.g. epics, Puranas) scripture.
Sacred sound or phrase used in worship and meditation, e.g. 'Om'.
Joseph Fletcher's situation ethics 1966 and Hans Kung's Global Ethic 1993 address abortion, euthanasia, IVF across traditions.
Five Precepts: refrain from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, intoxicants; complements Eightfold Path.
Cultivation of ren (humaneness), yi (righteousness), li (propriety), zhi (wisdom), xin (trustworthiness); five constant virtues.
Morality grounded in God's commands; Plato's Euthyphro 399 BCE poses dilemma: is the pious loved because pious, or pious because loved?
Gustavo Gutierrez's A Theology of Liberation 1971; preferential option for the poor; influenced Brazilian CEBs and Oscar Romero.
Thomas Aquinas's Summa Theologiae I-II q.94 (1265-74); eternal law accessible through reason; primary precepts of preservation, procreation, society.

hl-extension-philosophy-of-religion-argu.d: HL Extension: Philosophy of Religion (Arguments for/against God, Religious Language, Religious Experience)
terms: Negative theology of Pseudo-Dionysius c.500 CE and Meister Eckhart (d.1328); knows God by what God is not.
Teresa of Avila (d.1582) Interior Castle, John of the Cross (d.1591) Dark Night, Julian of Norwich (d.c.1416) Revelations.
Advaita non-dualism of Shankara (788-820); identifies Atman with Brahman; samadhi as direct realisation.
Das Heilige 1917 describes mysterium tremendum et fascinans; non-rational core of religion.
Rabia of Basra (d.801) introduced divine love; al-Hallaj (executed 922) declared 'Ana al-Haqq'; Rumi (d.1273) and Ibn Arabi (d.1240).
Varieties of Religious Experience 1902 Gifford Lectures; four marks of mystical experience: ineffability, noetic quality, transiency, passivity.
Judaism, Christianity, Islam; trace descent from Abraham; monotheistic; share Hebrew Bible/Torah and ethical monotheism.
Friedrich Max Muller's 1870 founding of comparative religion at Royal Institution; 'he who knows one knows none'.
Chinese family including Daoism, Confucianism and folk religion; emphasise harmony, yin-yang and ancestor veneration.
Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, Sikhism originating in Indian subcontinent; share karma, dharma and rebirth concepts.
Ninian Smart's Seven Dimensions of Religion 1989: doctrinal, mythical, ethical, ritual, experiential, social, material.
Emile Durkheim's Elementary Forms 1912: 'unified system of beliefs and practices relative to sacred things'; functionalist sociological approach.

introduction-to-religions-two-from-the-s.d: Introduction to Religions (Two from the SL list)
terms: Judaism, Christianity, Islam; trace descent from Abraham; monotheistic; share Hebrew Bible/Torah and ethical monotheism.
Friedrich Max Muller's 1870 founding of comparative religion at Royal Institution; 'he who knows one knows none'.
Chinese family including Daoism, Confucianism and folk religion; emphasise harmony, yin-yang and ancestor veneration.
Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, Sikhism originating in Indian subcontinent; share karma, dharma and rebirth concepts.
Ninian Smart's Seven Dimensions of Religion 1989: doctrinal, mythical, ethical, ritual, experiential, social, material.
Emile Durkheim's Elementary Forms 1912: 'unified system of beliefs and practices relative to sacred things'; functionalist sociological approach.
Oneness of God; the central doctrine of Islam expressed in the shahada.
Declaration of faith: 'There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the Messenger of God'.
Ritual prayer performed five times daily facing the Kaaba in Mecca.
Annual obligatory charitable giving, typically 2.5% of qualifying wealth.
Fasting from dawn to sunset during the month of Ramadan.
Pilgrimage to Mecca undertaken by Muslims able to do so once in a lifetime.
Majority branch of Islam (around 85-90%), affirming the legitimacy of the early caliphs.
Branch of Islam (about 10-13%) holding that leadership belonged to Ali and his descendants.
Shia doctrine of divinely guided successors of the Prophet, central to Shia identity.
Largest Shia branch, believing in 12 imams, the last in occultation.
Mystical dimension of Islam, present across Sunni and Shia traditions.
The recited Word of God revealed to Muhammad through the angel Jibril (Gabriel) from 610-632 CE.
Way and example of the Prophet Muhammad, preserved especially in the Hadith.
Recorded sayings, actions and approvals of the Prophet Muhammad, classified by reliability.
Major Sunni Hadith collection compiled by al-Bukhari (d. 870).
Qur'anic exegesis, the scholarly tradition of interpreting the Qur'an.
Islamic religious law derived from Qur'an, Sunnah, consensus (ijma) and analogy (qiyas).
Binding agreement initiated by God with chosen partners — Noah, Abraham, Moses, David.
Patriarch with whom God established a covenant (Genesis 12, 15, 17) and the rite of circumcision.
Leader who delivered the Israelites from Egypt and received the Torah at Sinai.
Liberation of the Israelites from slavery in Egypt, commemorated annually at Passover.
Covenant at Mount Sinai including the Ten Commandments and the Torah.
Commandments — traditionally 613 (248 positive and 365 negative) — structuring Jewish life.
Seventh-day rest from Friday sundown to Saturday sundown, commemorating Creation and Exodus.
Jewish dietary laws regulating which foods may be eaten and how they must be prepared.
Spring festival commemorating the Exodus, celebrated with the Seder meal.
Day of Atonement, the holiest day of the Jewish year, marked by fasting and prayer.
Jewish New Year, beginning the Ten Days of Awe culminating in Yom Kippur.
Hebrew term for the Holocaust, the genocide of approximately six million Jews 1933-45.
First five books of the Hebrew Bible: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy.
Hebrew Bible comprising Torah, Nevi'im (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings).
Compilation of Oral Torah edited by Judah ha-Nasi c. 200 CE.
Rabbinic commentary on the Mishnah; together with Mishnah forms the Talmud.
Central rabbinic work in two versions: the Jerusalem Talmud (c. 400) and the Babylonian Talmud (c. 500).
Genre of rabbinic interpretation expanding on biblical narrative and law.
Apparent contradiction between God's omnipotence, omnibenevolence and the existence of evil.
Claim that God's existence is logically incompatible with any evil.
Claim that the amount and distribution of evil makes God's existence unlikely.
Theodicy tracing evil to the misuse of free will by angels and humans (privatio boni).
Theodicy presenting evil as a means of moral and spiritual growth, developed by John Hick (soul-making).
Alvin Plantinga's argument that significant moral freedom necessarily allows the possibility of evil.
Encounter with the divine or transcendent that influences belief and action.
American philosopher-psychologist whose 1902 Varieties of Religious Experience analysed personal religion.
Experience marked by ineffability, noetic quality, transiency and passivity (James).
Rudolf Otto's term for the awe-inspiring 'mysterium tremendum et fascinans' of the holy.
Transformative religious experience associated with new commitment, e.g. Paul on the Damascus Road.
Argument that widespread reports of religious experience provide evidence for God.
View that humans are composed of two distinct substances, body and soul (Descartes).
Aristotelian view, adapted by Aquinas, that the soul is the form of the body.
View that humans consist solely of physical matter, denying a non-physical soul.
In Hindu thought, the eternal self or soul, ultimately identical with Brahman.
Buddhist doctrine of no-self: there is no permanent, unchanging soul.
Christian and Islamic belief in the bodily resurrection of the dead.
Bonds and trust that hold a community together; religions can foster both bonding and bridging capital.
Conflict in which religious identity, doctrine or institutions play a significant role.
Universal Declaration of Human Rights protecting freedom of thought, conscience and religion.
Laws criminalising speech offensive to religion; debated for freedom of expression implications.
Divisions and conflict between branches of the same religion, e.g. Sunni-Shia.
Restoration of relationships after conflict, often involving religious actors and rituals.
Form of government in which religious leaders rule in the name of divine authority, e.g. Iran post-1979.
French principle of strict separation of state and religion in public life.
Robert Bellah's concept of national religiosity surrounding the symbols of a state.
Reflection on the relation between religious doctrine and political life.
Movements fusing religious identity with political nationalism, e.g. Hindu nationalism in India.
Latin American theological movement (1960s-) emphasising God's preferential option for the poor.
Claim that modernisation produces decline in religious belief, practice and authority.
Sociologist defending a robust secularisation thesis (e.g. 'God is Dead', 2002).
Sociologist whose 1966 'Religion in Secular Society' analysed institutional decline.
Weber's concept of the modern erosion of magic and mystery from public life.
Peter Berger's revised view emphasising continuing religious vitality globally.
Coexistence of multiple religious traditions in a society.

internal-assessment-investigative-study-.d: Internal course: Investigative Study of a Religious Practice
terms: The emic view describes a practice from the insider's standpoint; the etic view analyses it from the outside using academic categories.
An internally assessed task requiring first-hand investigation of a religious practice and analysis of its meaning and significance for practitioners.
A research method in which the investigator attends a service, ritual or festival, observing carefully and recording what practitioners actually do.
Describing a religious practice as practitioners experience it, while bracketing the researcher's own assumptions and value judgements.
Primary sources include interviews, site visits and original texts; secondary sources are scholarly books and articles interpreting the practice.
Investigating living communities requires informed consent, sensitivity, confidentiality and respect for the beliefs and dignity of participants.

Annual observances such as Passover, Easter, Eid and Diwali that commemorate sacred events and renew communal identity through shared ritual.
Victor Turner described the liminal phase as a threshold state 'betwixt and between', generating communitas, an intense bond among participants.
A journey to a sacred site, such as the Hajj to Mecca or the Kumbh Mela, undertaken for devotion, purification or fulfilment of duty.
Rituals marking transitions between life stages, such as birth, coming of age, marriage and death ceremonies across religious traditions.
A patterned, repeated symbolic action — such as prayer, offering or procession — that expresses belief and binds a religious community together.
Arnold van Gennep analysed rites of passage as separation from the old status, a transitional (liminal) phase, and incorporation into the new status.
